questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=x^{3}+4x$.
The point $(5,1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
What is the equation of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at that point?

options.why: Used $f'(1)=7$ as the gradient instead of its reciprocal.
Used the point $(1,5)$, which lies on $y=f(x)$ rather than on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Both slips: gradient $7$ and the point $(1,5)$ from $y=f(x)$.

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=x^{5}+3x$.
The point $(4,1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
What is the equation of the normal to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at that point?

options.why: Gave the tangent instead of the normal.
Used $-\dfrac{1}{8}$ as the normal gradient instead of $-8$.
Used $+8$ as the normal gradient, dropping the negative sign.
Evaluated $f'$ at $7$ instead of at $1$, the value with $f(1)=7$.
Found $f'(1)=11$ correctly but did not take its reciprocal.
Used the given value $7$ in place of $f'(1)$.

questions.question_text:
The volume $V$ litres of water in a tank $t$ minutes after filling begins is $V=t^{2}+8t$.
What is $\dfrac{dt}{dV}$, in minutes per litre, when $V=20$?

options.why: Gave $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ instead of its reciprocal $\dfrac{dt}{dV}$.
Substituted $V=20$ into $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2t+8$ instead of the matching time $t=2$.
Used $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=8$, ignoring the $2t$ term.

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=3+\sqrt{x-2}$.
Which statement about the gradient of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $x=1$ is correct?

options.text: It does not exist, because the domain of $f^{-1}$ is $x\ge 3$ and $1$ lies outside it.
It does not exist, because $f'(1)=0$ at that point.
options.why: Tested $f'$ at $1$, but $1$ is not even in the domain of $f$, and $f'$ is never zero here.
Used the domain endpoint $3$ instead of recognising that $x=1$ is outside the domain of $f^{-1}$.

options.text: It is $0$, because $f^{-1}(1)$ is undefined and so the curve is flat there.
options.why: Treated an undefined value as a gradient of zero.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{x-2}\ge 0$, so the range of $f$ is $y\ge 3$.
The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, so it is $x\ge 3$.
$x=1$ lies outside this domain, so no point of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ has $x=1$ and the gradient does not exist.

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x)=x^{3}+6x-3$.
What is the equation of the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point where $x=4$?

options.why: Used $f'(1)=9$ as the gradient instead of its reciprocal.
Used the point $(1,4)$, which lies on $y=f(x)$ rather than on $y=f^{-1}(x)$.
Both slips: gradient $9$ and the point $(1,4)$ from $y=f(x)$.
Evaluated $f'$ at $2$ instead of at $0$, the value with $f(0)=2$.
Found $f'(0)=3$ correctly but did not take its reciprocal.
Used $f'(x)=2e^{x}$, forgetting to differentiate the $+x$ term.

questions.question_text:
The normal to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(10,4)$ has equation $y=-6x+64$.
What is $f'(4)$?

options.why: Quoted the normal gradient itself rather than working back to $f'(4)$.
Gave $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(10)$, the tangent gradient, instead of $f'(4)$.
Took the reciprocal of the normal gradient without changing its sign.

questions.solution_text:
The normal has gradient $-6$, so the tangent to $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $(10,4)$ has gradient $\dfrac{1}{6}$.
$(10,4)$ on $f^{-1}$ means $f(4)=10$, so $\left(f^{-1}\right)'(10)=\dfrac{1}{f'(4)}$.
$\dfrac{1}{f'(4)}=\dfrac{1}{6}$
$f'(4)=6$
